d: A Japanese pinball game played on a vertical board
ety: Borrowed from Japanese パチンコ (pachinko), from ぱちん (pachin, onomatopoeic sound of the machines) + こ (ko, diminutive). Compare etymology of gacha, from Japanese ガシャポン.
s: Snow filled her mouth. She caromed off things she never saw, tumbling through a cluttered canyon like a steel marble falling through pins in a pachinko machine.

d: Take hold of; grab
ety: From Latin prehendere. See prehensile.
s: Each of the four levels "prehends" the other, and so in the punning of words so frequent in hieroglyphic writing, we encounter a richer and more inclusive mode of thought than we are accustomed to.

d: Fortification consisting of a strong fence made of stakes driven into the ground
ety: Borrowed from Middle French palissade, from Old French, from Old Occitan palissada, from palissa (“stake”), probably from pal (“stake”), or possibly from Gallo-Romance *pālīcea, from Latin pālus (“stake”) + -ade.
s: Before the clearing had been half crossed the Arabs opened up a withering fire from behind the palisade.

d: Impossible to satisfy
ety: From Late Middle English insaciate, insaciat, insacyate (“insatiable”), from Latin insatiātus, from in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + satiātus (“satisfied; having been satisfied”) (perfect passive participle of satiō (“to satisfy”), from satis (“enough; filled; plenty”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂- (“to satiate, satisfy”)) + -ō (suffix forming regular first-conjugation verbs)).
s: I shuddered to think who might be the next victim sacrificed to his insatiate revenge.

d: A colonnade surrounding a building or enclosing a court
ety: From French péristyle, from Classical Latin peristȳlum, from Ancient Greek περίστυλον (perístulon), from περι- (peri-, “around”) + στῦλος (stûlos, “pillar”), equivalent to peri- + -style.
s: The peristyle is a roofed structure, open at the sides, in which most of the ceremonials and dances take place.

d: Offensively self-assured or given to exercising usually unwarranted power
ety: From Anglo-Norman peremptorie, parentorie et al. (Modern French péremptoire), and its source, Latin peremptōrius (“deadly; precluding debate, decisive”), from perimō (“destroy, thwart”), from per- (“thorough”) + emō (“to obtain, buy”).
s: As this trial has now been postponed multiple times, there will be an adjournment to April 24, peremptory on the parties.

d: Marked by up-to-dateness in dress and manners
ety: From Middle English daper (“pretty, neat”), from Middle Dutch dapper (“stalwart, nimble”), Old Dutch *dapar, from Proto-Germanic *dapraz (“stout; solid; heavy; bold”) (compare German tapfer "bold", Norwegian daper "saddened, dreary"), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeb- ‘thick, heavy’ (compare Tocharian A tpär ‘high’, Latvian dàbls ‘strong’, Serbo-Croatian дебео (dèbeo) ‘fat’).
s: Going down the street, you would meet a typical commercial traveller, dapper and alert.

d: A manual of black magic (for invoking spirits and demons)
ety: Borrowed from French grimoire, a variant of grammaire, from Old French gramaire (“grammar; grimoire; conjurer, magician”), from Latin grammatica (“grammar; philology”), from grammaticus (“relating to grammar, grammatical”), from Ancient Greek γρᾰμμᾰτῐκός (grămmătĭkós, “knowing one's letters; concerned with textual criticism”), from γράμμα (grámma, “that which is drawn or written; letter; book, wri
s: Nevertheless, to generations of writers after Independence, the printed word was a kind of magic, the grimoire that would bring about liberation.

d: A persistent but subordinate motif
ety: From Italian obbligato. Piecewise doublet of obliged.
s: The noise of the traffic outside the building on the boulevard made an unmusical obbligato to my thinking.

d: High-flown style; excessive use of verbal ornamentation
ety: From Middle French grandiloquence, from Latin grandiloquentia, from grandiloquus, 1580s.
s: The grandiosity of his prose.

d: A serpent (or lizard or dragon) able to kill with its breath or glance
ety: From Middle English basilicke, borrowed from Old French basilique, from Latin basiliscus, from Ancient Greek βασιλίσκος (basilískos, literally “minor king or chieftain”), from βασιλεύς (basileús, “king”), possibly based on descriptions or rare encounters with different types of cobra which have crown-like patterns on their head; the 'deadly gaze' may have been from the spitting cobra's ability to
s: As a guide to start your collection we'd suggest either iguanas, tejus, swifts, basilisks, horned toads or alligator lizards.

d: The loyalty that citizens owe to their country (or subjects to their sovereign)
ety: Inherited from Middle English feaute, feute, from Anglo-Norman fëauté, fëuté, from Latin fidēlitās (“faithfulness”; “homage, fealty” in Medieval Latin), from fidēlis (“faithful”) + -tās (noun suffix); the modern form (for expected *feauty /ˈfjuːti/) is due to learned influence. Equivalent to obsolete feal + -ty. Doublet of fidelity.
s: I think the central characteristic Trump seems to be looking for in all of the appointees we’ve seen so far is fealty to him.

d: A wide (ornamented) belt worn over the right shoulder to support a sword or bugle by the left hip
ety: From Middle English baudrik, bauderik, baudry (“belt worn over the shoulder or around the waist for carrying a sword, etc., baldric; (by extension) type of leather strap”), from Old French baldré, baldrei, baudré (“crossbelt, sword-belt”) (modern French baudrier); further etymology uncertain, possibly from Frankish *balterād, from earlier *baltiraidī (“belt gear, belt equipment”) (compare Old Occi
s: And from his blazon'd baldric slung, / A mighty silver bugle hung, / And, as he rode, his armour rung, / Beside remote Shalott.

d: A blank leaf in the front or back of a book
ety: From fly + leaf.
s: The scribbles on the margins, the occasional date on the flyleaf, the faded bus ticket marking a page for a reason today mysterious, all try to remind me of who I was then.

d: A person who is not very intelligent or interested in culture
ety: From Dutch boomken (“shrub, little tree”), equivalent to boom + -kin. Note that the English word boom is etymologically related to the aforementioned in the sense of "large stem", or "big tree". Compare German Baumke, Bäumchen.
s: They mix with Dancers, who now advance to the front, where a bumpkin, or dance of many interwoven reels, is performed; after which the Bride is led to a seat, and some of her Maidens sit by her.

d: A patterned wood inlay used to cover a floor
ety: From parquet + -ry.
s: The new ballroom floor is a marvellous example of parquetry.

d: Cause to be bitter or resentful
ety: From Middle English envenymen, from Old French envenimer (“to poison, taint”); equivalent to en- + venom.
s: Ah dearest, whoso sucks a poisoned wound Envenoms his own veins!

d: A heavy cannon with a long barrel used in the 16th and 17th centuries
ety: From Middle English culveryne, from Old French coulevrine, from couleuvre (“snake”) (or from Latin colubrīnus), ultimately from Latin colubra, coluber (“snake”). Doublet of colubrine.
s: This had been discharged from a culverin on the opposite side of the valley.

d: With little or no preparation or forethought
ety: Univerbation of Latin ex tempore. First attested before 1556.
s: Sheets, tablecloths, white gowns, and pocket-handkerchiefs were instantly in demand, and every one, as has been seen, entered, con amore, into the extempore entertainment of Pandemonic Revels.

d: Treat or speak of with contempt
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin dērīdēre, the present active infinitive of dērīdeō (“to laugh at, make fun of, mock, deride”), from dē- (prefix denoting putting down or subjecting to indignity) + rīdeō (“to laugh; to laugh at, mock, ridicule”) (further etymology uncertain, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *wert- (“to rotate; to turn”) (referring to turning the mouth to smile) or *wreyd- (“to carve;
s: He derided his student's attempt to solve the biggest problem in mathematics.

d: A list of proper nouns naming persons or places
ety: From Ancient Greek ὀνομαστικόν (onomastikón), neuter form of ὀνομαστικός (onomastikós, “belonging to names”), from ὀνομάζω (onomázō, “I name”), from ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”). The term onomastikón (collection of names, from ὄνομα/ónoma, ‘name’) describes learned works that are not arranged alphabetically but juxtapose synonyms and terms relating to the same semantic field. This principle of ordering i
s: We looked up the origin of her name in an onomasticon.

d: Beg persistently and urgently
ety: From Middle French importuner and its etymon Medieval Latin importūnor (“to make oneself troublesome”), from Latin importūnus (“unfit, troublesome”), originally "having no harbor".
s: But I will no longer importune my young cousin.

d: Ignorance (especially of orthodox beliefs)
ety: From Latin nescientia, from the present participle of nescire.
s: Better to have honest nescience than to have militant ignorance.

d: A small vehicle with four wheels in which a baby or child is pushed around
ety: From perambulate + -or.
s: The reapers were slowly trooping back to their work. The nurse-girl slapped one of her charges and then began to push the perambulator up the hill.

d: Lacking or showing a lack of due concern
ety: From Middle English blithe (“glad, happy, joyful; causing joy, joyous; gentle, mild; gracious, merciful; bright, shining; beautiful, fair”) [and other forms], from Old English blīþe (“happy, gentle”), from Proto-West Germanic *blīþī, from Proto-Germanic *blīþiz (“friendly; gentle, mild; pleasing”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlī- (“fine; light; pleasant”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“shiny;
s: She had a blithe disregard of cultures outside the United States.

d: Used of the study of a phenomenon (especially language) as it changes through time
ety: By surface analysis, dia- + chron- + -ic; historically, see synchronous § Etymology.
s: In short, it's usual for the syuzhet to appear more diachronic at the beginning and more synchronic at the end.

d: A formal and solemn declaration of objection
ety: From Old French protestacion, from Latin prōtestātiō.
s: October 28, 1552, Hugh Latimer, Sermon on the Gospel for St Simon and St Jude's Day The protestation of our faith.

d: A wild and exciting undertaking (not necessarily lawful)
ety: Borrowed from French escapade (“the act of escaping; a trick”), itself borrowed from Old Spanish escapada, from escapar (“to escape”), from Vulgar Latin *excappāre.
s: He seems on the verge of winning the New York Senate election when the New York Post runs a photo of David’s exposed butt in a mooning escapade from his college days.

d: Without material form or substance
ety: From Latin incorporeus + -al. By surface analysis, in- + corporeal.
s: Thus incorporeal spirits to smaller forms / Reduced their shapes immense.

d: Lacking spirit or liveliness
ety: From the archaic expression lackadaisy + -ic + -al.
s: I could hear the sound of the janitor's lackadaisical scrubbing against the wooden floor.

d: The personal outfit of a bride; clothes and accessories and linens
ety: Borrowed from French trousseau, diminutive of trousse (“bundle”).
s: Consequently, having decided to divide her daughter's trousseau into two parts, a lesser and a larger, the Princess eventually consented to have the wedding before Advent.

d: A flat stone for sharpening edged tools or knives
ety: From Middle English whestone, whetston, whetesston, from Old English hwetstān, from Proto-West Germanic *hwattjastain (“whetstone”). Equivalent to whet (“to sharpen”) + stone.
s: It was as if a stone were ground to dust; as if white sparks flew from a livid whetstone, which was his spine; as if the switchback railway, having swooped to the depths, fell, fell, fell.

d: The main tower within the walls of a medieval castle or fortress
ety: A variant of dungeon remodelled on its etymon, Old French donjon.
s: ‘Start bearding one of these barons in his own castle and next thing you’re being bounced down to the donjon keep.’

d: Any vertical post or rod used as a support
ety: From Old French estanson, estanchon, (Modern French étançon), from estance (“a stay, a prop”), from Latin stāns (“standing”), present participle of stō.
s: The train began to move. Lace walked with it, holding a stanchion.

d: A structure that has a roof and walls and stands more or less permanently in one place
ety: From Middle English edifice, from Old French edifice, a classical borrowing of Latin aedificium (“building”), derived from aedificāre (“to build, establish”) (whence also English edify).
s: With a great thump on the table, Poirot demolished his carefully built up edifice.

d: Branched candlestick; ornamental; has several lights
ety: Unadapted borrowing from Latin candēlābrum (“candlestick”), from candēla. Doublet of chandelier. Displaced native Old English candeltrēow (literally “candle tree”).
s: Cyby followed us holding up his candelabrum—I suppose more for his benefit than mine, but it permitted me to see well enough to keep from colliding with the dark oak shelves we passed.

d: Be a signal for or a symptom of
ety: From Middle English bespeken, bispeken, from Old English *bespecan, besprecan (“to speak about, speak against, accuse of, claim at law, complain”), from Proto-West Germanic *bisprekan (“to discuss, blame”), from Proto-Germanic *bisprekaną (“to speak about, discuss, blame”), equivalent to be- + speak. Cognate with Scots bespeke (“to beseech, speak or negotiate with”), Saterland Frisian bispreke (“t
s: This act bespeaks his kindness.

d: A solemn supplication ceremony prescribed by the church
ety: Borrowed from Latin rogātiō, from rogō (“request”). By surface analysis, Latin rog- + -ate + -ion.
s: He perfecteth the rogations or litanies before in use.

d: A triangular fore-and-aft sail used especially in the Mediterranean
ety: From French latine (“Latin”).
s: The lateen sail is triangular or a quadrilateral which is almost triangular, the former being the type used by the Byzantines.

d: Add details, as to an account or idea; clarify the meaning of and discourse in a learned way, usually in writing
ety: From Middle English expounden, from Old French espondre, from Latin exponere. Doublet of expone and expose.
s: Today I'll expound at length the theory propounded last week.
